section.name: AI claims explained
section.introduction: Six claims you'll hear about AI, checked against the evidence for readers in the United States. See what each one means, how much hype it carries, and what you can do if you're concerned.
section.scoreNote: Hype scores check the wording of a claim against the evidence. They don't measure how serious or likely a harm is. Unlike feed stories, these pages don't show evidence-gap flags yet; the limits of the evidence are described in words.
section.feedInvitationTitle: Concerned about a recurring AI claim?
section.feedInvitationBody: Explore the evidence on water, jobs, climate, creativity, privacy, and existential risk.

water.keyQualification: Depends on the local water source, cooling and hot-day demand; not every data center causes shortages.
publicEvidenceLimitations: Most national figures cover all data centers, not just AI.
We lack good data on individual facilities and hot-day use, and forecasts of strain aren’t proof that households will go without.
water.scope: Particular US towns where water is tight; not every data center, and not the whole country.
water.timeHorizon: Current and planned data centers; no deadline.

jobs.keyQualification: A possible scenario from May 2025 for roughly 2026–2030; the half-of-jobs number is untested and isn’t a forecast for you.
publicEvidenceLimitations: Job and hiring data can’t yet show how much AI is the cause.
How fast companies adopt AI, and the size and timing of any job losses, are uncertain.
jobs.scope: Entry-level office jobs in the US; not all jobs, and not your own prospects.
jobs.timeHorizon: One to five years from May 2025, so roughly 2026–2030.

energy-climate.keyQualification: Means more emissions than without AI’s extra demand; total US emissions could still fall.
publicEvidenceLimitations: Companies share little data on AI’s own energy use, and US and worldwide estimates cover different things.
Future emissions depend on demand, efficiency, how power is made, and whether AI’s possible climate benefits happen.
energy-climate.scope: US carbon emissions from electricity, compared with a US without AI’s extra demand.

creativity.keyQualification: Shown in chosen models and tests; not every output is copied, and not all training is illegal.
publicEvidenceLimitations: Targeted tests don’t show how often copying happens in everyday use.
The job and court findings each cover specific people, facts and places.
creativity.scope: AI tools available to US users; copying in AI answers, not every use of training data.
creativity.timeHorizon: Now, based on evidence through October 6, 2026.

privacy.keyQualification: About ChatGPT personal accounts and OpenAI’s stated rules; training settings don’t control storage, access or sharing.
publicEvidenceLimitations: Company policies say what should happen, not what independent checks have confirmed.
Other chatbots, workplace setups and state rights need separate checks.
privacy.scope: ChatGPT personal accounts for US users, compared with business accounts.

existential-risk.keyQualification: A prediction about future superintelligent AI, with no deadline; certain extinction isn’t shown by the evidence.
publicEvidenceLimitations: Today’s tests and incidents don’t show how AI could lead to permanent, worldwide loss of control.
Expert estimates are opinions, and big questions about future AI, defenses and recovery are still open.
existential-risk.scope: Worldwide; future superintelligent AI built with methods like those of 2025.
